questions.q: What was the point of the structured checkpoint logging built in course 7, from the perspective of this lesson?
options: It creates a trail — specific values at defined points — that makes a production failure diagnosable months later instead of starting from a blank screen
It automatically fixes any integration failure without human review
It replaces the need for the Slow Request Log or Script Performance Profiler entirely
It only matters while the integration is first being built, not afterward
questions.explain: Checkpoint logging exists precisely so that a later production failure has specific evidence to read back, not a vague symptom report.

questions.q: The Script Performance Profiler shows that almost all the time in a failing integration transaction is spent inside your own transform script, before any outbound call is made. What does this suggest?
options: The cause is more likely a genuine bug in your own code than an external system problem
The external system is definitely rate-limiting your requests
This always means an OAuth token has expired
The Script Performance Profiler cannot be used on integration code
questions.explain: Time sunk in your own script, before the call ever leaves the instance, points at your own logic rather than something outside your control.

questions.q: A checkpoint log shows every recent call to a third-party API returning HTTP 429. What is the correct response?
options: Adjust call volume or backoff timing — the external system is telling you to slow down, not rejecting the request for a logic reason
Rewrite the transform script that builds the request body
Assume the OAuth token has expired and refresh the credential
Conclude there is no real problem and take no action
questions.explain: HTTP 429 specifically means rate-limiting. The fix is about call volume/timing, not request-building logic or credentials.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say that diving straight into the script editor can waste real incident time when a production integration fails?
options: Because if the real cause is external (an outage, rate-limiting, an expired token), no code change can fix it, and the time would be better spent confirming the cause and communicating status
Because editing scripts in production is technically disabled by the platform
Because the Script Performance Profiler always finds the bug faster than reading logs
Because external causes are extremely rare in practice
questions.explain: The core point is the diagnostic fork: external causes need a completely different response than a code fix, so confirming which one it is comes first.

questions.q: A call fails with an HTTP 401 even though the checkpoint log confirms the request payload was built exactly as expected. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: An expired or invalid OAuth token — the fix is refreshing or reconfiguring the credential, not debugging the payload
A business rule recursive loop, fixable by adding an update condition
An index missing on the target table, fixable by adding one
A semaphore pool exhaustion issue, fixable by increasing node count
questions.explain: A correctly built request that still fails authentication is the classic signature of an expired or invalid credential, not a logic or performance problem.
